title: Methods of increasing fish production

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the basement of a building in Baltimore's inner harbour, a group of aquaculturists at the Institute of Marine and Environmental Technology in Maryland, USA, is creating an artificial ecosystem. These researchers hope to liberate the farming of ocean fish from the ocean itself so that fish farms can be built inland. People have raised freshwater fish in ponds for many centuries, but farming species such as salmon that live mainly in salty water has only been attempted in the past few decades, as has the parallel transformation of freshwater aquaculture to operate on an industrial scale. Now fish farming is booming and numbers show that human consumption of fish produced through farming has overtaken that of other food types. Indeed, one way of supplying humankind with enough animal protein in future may be through aquaculture. To keep the boom going, though, technologists must become ever more inventive. Yonathan Zohar works at the Institute of Marine and Environmental Technology. His ecosystem constantly recycles the same supply of brine (salty water), purified by three sets of bacteria. One set turns ammonia excreted by the fish into nitrate ions. A second converts these ions into nitrogen (a harmless gas that makes up 78% of the air) and water. A third, working on the solid waste filtered from the water, transforms it into methane, which – via a portable generator – provides part of the power that keeps the whole operation running. The outcome is a closed system that can be set up anywhere and generates no pollution. It is also escape-proof, to prevent possible breeding outside the enclosure. That means old-world species such as sea bream and sea bass, which now cannot be farmed because they might get out, could be delivered fresh to the table anywhere.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Fish farmers used to dream of fitting their fish with transgenes to make them grow more quickly. Indeed, over the past couple of decades researchers have treated more than 35 fish species in this way. They have often been spectacularly successful. Only one firm, though, has persisted to the point of obtaining regulatory approval. AquaBounty's transgenic Atlantic salmon, now cleared in both the United States and Canada, has the desirable property of rapid growth. Its transgene, taken from a chinook salmon, causes it to put on weight all year round, not just in spring and summer. That halves the time the fish will take to reach marketable size.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: However, there is so much natural variation in wild fish that conventional selective breeding can make a big difference without any high-tech intervention. Back in 2007 a report by researchers at Akvaforsk, now part of the Norwegian Institute of Food, Fisheries and Aquaculture Research (NOFIMA), showed that selective breeding by the country's salmon farmers had resulted in fish which grew twice as quickly as their wild progenitors. Admittedly starting from a lower base, those farmers had done what AquaBounty has achieved, but without the aid of a transgene.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: If conventional selection can produce such improvements, it is tempting not to bother with anything more complicated. Tempting, but wrong. For, as understanding of fish DNA improves, the sort of genetic selection being applied to crops like corn or wheat can also be applied to fish. Researchers at SalmoBreed of Bergen, in Norway, have employed genetic selection not to create bigger, faster-growing fish but to attack two of fish farming's banes – infestation and infection. By tracking a particular part of a gene, they have produced varieties of salmon resistant to sea lice and also to pancreas disease and other viral illnesses.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Altering nature, then, is crucial to the success of fish farming. But nurture can also give a helping hand, for example by optimising what is fed to the animals. As with any product, one key to success is to keep costs down. And here, environmental and commercial considerations coincide. A common complaint is that fish farming does not relieve as much pressure on the oceans as it appears to, because a lot of the feed it uses is made of fish meal. That simply transfers fishing pressure from species eaten by people directly to those that get turned into such meal. But fish meal is expensive, so researchers have successfully reduced the amount being used by substituting plant matter, such as soya.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Feeding carnivores like salmon on plants is one way to reduce not just costs but also environmental harm. Another way, which at first sight seems exotic, is to make fish food out of natural gas. This is the business of Calysta, a Californian firm. Calysta feeds the gas – or, rather, its principal component, methane – to bacteria called methanotrophs. These metabolise the methane, extract energy from it and use the atoms thus liberated, along with oxygen from water and nitrogen from the air, to build their bodies. Calysta then turns these bodies into protein pellets that are sold as fish food, a process that puts no strain at all on either sea or land. Even conventional fish foods, though, are more economical and environmentally friendly compared with feed for livestock. Because fish are cold-blooded, they do not have to eat to stay warm. They thus convert more of their food into body mass. For conservationists, and for those who worry whether there will be enough food in future to feed the growing human population, that makes fish a particularly attractive form of animal protein.
